# Sharing one Postgres between go-boot and Spring Data JPA

Legwork for [#13](https://github.com/squall-chua/go-boot/issues/13). Date: 2026-08-24.
Toolchain: `go1.26.3`, OpenJDK 25.0.3, Hibernate ORM 6.6.11.Final, PostgreSQL 18.3, all
linux/amd64.

**Nothing here was read from a blog.** Every schema below was generated by running Hibernate, and
every behaviour below was observed by running two writers against one live database. Two of the
findings contradict what I expected before testing, and both are marked.

---

## 1. What a Spring Boot service actually creates

These entity fields:

```java
@Entity public class Customer {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;      // the DEFAULT strategy
    @Version private Long version;
    private String firstName;
    private boolean isActive;
    private UUID externalRef;
    private Instant createdAt;
    private LocalDateTime updatedAt;
    @Enumerated private Status status;                       // DEFAULT
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) private Status statusAsText;
}
@Entity public class OrderLine {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
    private BigDecimal unitPrice;
    private int quantityOrdered;
}
```

produce this, via `jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.scripts.action=create` with
`hibernate.physical_naming_strategy=org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy`:

```sql
create sequence customer_seq start with 1 increment by 50;
create table customer (
    id bigint not null, version bigint,
    first_name varchar(255), email_address varchar(255), is_active boolean not null,
    external_ref uuid, created_at timestamp(6) with time zone, updated_at timestamp(6),
    status smallint check (status between 0 and 2),
    status_as_text varchar(255) check (status_as_text in ('NEW','ACTIVE','CLOSED')),
    primary key (id));
create table order_line (
    id bigint generated by default as identity,
    quantity_ordered integer not null, unit_price numeric(38,2), primary key (id));
```

The naming strategy is the Spring Boot default, not a Hibernate one. Raw Hibernate leaves names
alone and produces `create table Customer (... firstName ...)`. Spring Boot's documentation
states: *"By default, Spring Boot configures the physical naming strategy with
`CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy`... all dots are replaced by underscores and camel casing is
replaced by underscores as well. Additionally, by default, all table names are generated in lower
case."*
([Spring Boot how-to: data access](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-access.html))

**This matters for go-boot because it is the good news.** `first_name`, `created_at`,
`order_line` is already what a Go service and sqlc would have written. The naming is free.

---

## 2. The convention table

| JPA declaration | Column it creates | What the Go side must do |
|---|---|---|
| naming (Spring Boot default) | `Customer` → `customer`, `firstName` → `first_name` | nothing — already matches |
| `@Version` | `version bigint` | **must** write `version = version + 1` on every update (§4) |
| `@Id @GeneratedValue` (default) | sequence, `increment by 50` | `nextval` is safe (§3), but burns 50 ids per row |
| `@GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)` | `generated by default as identity` | **prefer** — plain `INSERT … RETURNING id` |
| `@Enumerated` (default) | `smallint check (x between 0 and N)` | **avoid** — the integer is the Java enum's declaration order |
| `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` | `varchar(255)` + a value CHECK | **use this** |
| `Instant` | `timestamp(6) with time zone` | maps cleanly |
| `LocalDateTime` | `timestamp(6)`, no zone | avoid — the offset is lost |
| `UUID` | `uuid` | pgx handles it |
| `BigDecimal` | `numeric(38,2)` | needs a Go decimal type; `float64` is wrong |

---

## 3. The shared sequence is safe — **this contradicts what I expected**

The hypothesis was that Hibernate's pooled optimizer, holding a block of 50 ids in memory, would
collide with a Go writer calling `nextval` on the same sequence.

**It does not.** Both writers ran at the same time, 40 rows each, into one `customer` table:

- **80 rows inserted, zero duplicate keys, zero failed inserts.**
- Hibernate took `2152`–`2191` — one `nextval`, then 50 ids handed out from memory.
- Go took `201, 251, 301, … 2151` — one `nextval` per row, each burning a whole block.

The reason is that Hibernate derives every block from a real `nextval`, and so does Go. Two
clients calling `nextval` on the same sequence cannot receive overlapping ranges. The blocks
interleave; they never overlap.

The real cost is waste, not correctness: **Go spends 50 id values per row**, because the sequence's
`increment by` is 50. Go's 40 rows consumed the range 201 to 2151. With `bigint` that is
irrelevant. With a 4-byte `serial` it would not be.

**Recommendation: use `GenerationType.IDENTITY` on the JPA side anyway.** It produces
`generated by default as identity`, which lets the Go side do `INSERT … RETURNING id` with no
waste and no shared-sequence reasoning at all.

---

## 4. `@Version` is the one that loses data

The scenario is the ordinary one: a Hibernate transaction reads a row and starts editing it, and a
Go service writes the same row before Hibernate commits.

**Case A — Go updates without touching `version`:**

```
GO   updated 1 row(s), mode=blind
HIBERNATE commit OK
FINAL first_name=JPA-WROTE-THIS
```

Hibernate's update is `... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`. Go left `version` alone, so the
predicate still matches, the update succeeds, and **Go's write is silently destroyed. No error is
raised anywhere.**

**Case B — Go also does `version = version + 1`:**

```
GO   updated 1 row(s), mode=bump
HIBERNATE REFUSED: StaleObjectStateException
FINAL first_name=GO-WROTE-THIS
```

Hibernate's predicate no longer matches, so it raises the optimistic-lock failure it exists to
raise, and Go's write survives.

**One line of SQL is the difference between working concurrency control and silent data loss.**
This is the single most important rule for a shared schema.

---

## 5. Migration ownership: exactly one owner

Each tool writes its own bookkeeping table, and two tools both trying to own a schema will fight:

| tool | table |
|---|---|
| goose | `goose_db_version` |
| Flyway | `flyway_schema_history` |
| Liquibase | `databasechangelog`, `databasechangeloglock` |

go-boot supports the "JPA side owns the schema" case with no extra code: passing a nil migrations
`fs.FS` to `db.New` skips both the migration and the `HasPending` refusal, leaving a pool and a
readiness Check. See ADR 0007.

---

## 6. Hibernate's own validator — necessary, **not sufficient**

`spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate` is the authoritative check, because only Hibernate knows
what Hibernate expects. I ran it against six schemas built by goose-style SQL:

| schema handed to Hibernate | `validate` result |
|---|---|
| exact match | `PASS` |
| `version` column missing | `FAIL -> Schema-validation: missing column [version] in table [customer]` |
| whole table missing | `FAIL -> Schema-validation: missing table [order_line]` |
| sequence missing | `FAIL -> Schema-validation: missing sequence [customer_seq]` |
| `timestamp` where JPA wants `timestamp with time zone` | **`PASS`** |
| `varchar(10)` where JPA wants `varchar(255)` | **`PASS`** |

**This also contradicts what I expected.** `validate` checks that things are *present* — tables,
columns, sequences. It does not check column types or lengths. Both of the failures that corrupt
data or reject writes at runtime pass validation silently.

So a go-boot-side lint has a real job: the gap list is `timestamp` without a time zone, identifiers
that are not lower_snake_case, a smallint column with a `between 0 and N` check, and a table with
no `version` column. That lint checks a **convention**, not a JPA model — go-boot cannot read Java
classes and must never claim otherwise.

---

## Recommendation

**Let one side own the schema, and prefer the JPA side when a JPA service already exists.** That
removes the verification problem instead of solving it: there is one source of truth, Hibernate can
generate and validate its own schema, and go-boot runs with `migrations = nil`.

When go-boot must own the schema, the CI recipe is: start a Postgres, run goose, then boot the Java
service with `ddl-auto=validate` — and know from §6 that this leaves types unchecked.

## Reproduction

Everything above was run from a scratch directory: 16 Hibernate jars pulled from Maven Central, the
PostgreSQL 18.3 binaries that `fergusstrange/embedded-postgres` caches, and a small Go writer. No
part of it touched this repository, and nothing was added to any `go.mod` here.

## Addendum: the lint's test fixture (2026-08-25, [#27](https://github.com/squall-chua/go-boot/issues/27))

`LintJPAConventions` has to be tested against a schema Hibernate itself generated, so one was
generated. **Hibernate ORM 7.4.1.Final**, OpenJDK 25.0.3, jars already on disk, no network. This is
a **newer Hibernate than the 6.6.11 used above**, because 6.6.11 was no longer on this machine.

The entities follow this page — `@Version` on both, `IDENTITY` ids, `Instant` rather than
`LocalDateTime`, `@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)` — with
`hibernate.physical_naming_strategy=CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy` (the Spring Boot default)
and `jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.scripts.action=create`. The output is checked in verbatim
at `db/dbtest/testdata/hibernate_schema.sql`, and the lint reports nothing against it.

**One difference from §1's 6.6.11 output**, and it is the only one: 7.4.1 writes
`version bigint not null`, where 6.6.11 wrote `version bigint`. Nothing the lint or this page
depends on.

A schema Hibernate generated is **not** automatically clean. §1's own `customer`, from the default
entity set, has `updated_at timestamp(6)` from a `LocalDateTime` — which is exactly what the lint
flags. Clean means the entities followed this page, not that Hibernate wrote the DDL.
